definition: To fail to notice or think about something, especially something that matters.
example: Dazzled by the ocean view, the buyers overlooked the cracks in the old porch steps.
nuance: Overlooking is usually accidental, unlike ignoring; do not confuse it with oversee (to supervise) or look over (to examine).
prompt: A team is checking a budget spreadsheet before sending it to the school board.
options: Check the formulas again, since it's easy to overlook one misplaced decimal point.
Our treasurer will overlook the budget team and approve each person's work.
Please overlook every cell carefully so that no wrong number slips through.
When you overlook a missing receipt, circle it in red so we can find it later.
reasons: A tiny decimal error is exactly the kind of detail people miss without meaning to.
Supervising a group and approving work is what oversee means, not overlook.
Examining something closely is looking it over; overlooking is what lets errors slip through.
You can't mark something you failed to notice, so this treats the word as if it meant spotting.

practice.prompt: A student is reading the entry rules for a science fair.
options: The rules overlook how big each poster can be, listing exact measurements in inches.
Read the rules twice so you don't overlook the limit on poster size.
To overlook the safety guidelines, Lena highlighted each one and taped them above her desk.
Kenji asked his teacher to overlook his draft and suggest a few improvements.
reasons: Rules that give exact measurements clearly address poster size instead of leaving it out.
Rereading protects against missing a small but important requirement.
Highlighting and posting the rules shows close attention, which is the reverse of missing them.
Reviewing a draft for feedback is looking it over; overlooking it would mean not noticing it at all.
